title: 2-D DP: Edit Distance
oneLiner: The fewest single-character inserts, deletes and replaces to turn one word into another -- the classic two-string DP table.
keyTakeaway: dp[i][j] = the cost to turn the first i characters of a into the first j characters of b. If a[i-1] == b[j-1] it's free: dp[i-1][j-1]. Otherwise it's 1 + the cheapest of replace (dp[i-1][j-1]), delete (dp[i-1][j]) and insert (dp[i][j-1]). Row 0 and column 0 are just 0..n.
explanation:
Spell-check suggestions, diff tools and DNA alignment all need a number for "how different are these two strings?". Edit distance (Levenshtein distance) is the minimum number of single-character edits -- insert, delete or replace -- that turns one into the other. kitten → sitting is 3: replace k with s, replace e with i, insert g.

Whenever a problem compares two sequences, try a 2-D table indexed by "how much of each have I used". Here dp[i][j] is the edit distance between a's first i characters and b's first j. The edges are easy: turning i characters into nothing takes i deletes, so dp[i][0] = i, and dp[0][j] = j inserts. For any other cell, look at the last characters. If they match, they cost nothing and dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]. If they don't, the last step was one of three edits: replace a's last character with b's (1 + dp[i-1][j-1]), delete a's last character (1 + dp[i-1][j]), or insert b's last character (1 + dp[i][j-1]). Take the cheapest.

Fill the table row by row, left to right, so every cell's three neighbours (up, left, up-left) are already known. The answer is the bottom-right cell, dp[len(a)][len(b)]. Since each row only needs the row above, you can keep just two rows if memory matters.

The visualization fills the table for kitten → sitting one row at a time.

visualizationSteps.message: Row 0: turning the empty string into the first j characters of "sitting" takes j inserts.
Row 1 ('k'): no letter of "sitting" matches 'k', so every cell is 1 + min(replace, delete, insert).
Row 2 ('i'): highlighted cells are where 'i' matches a letter of "sitting", so they copy the diagonal for free. Every other cell is 1 + min(up-left, up, left).
Row 3 ('t'): highlighted cells are where 't' matches a letter of "sitting", so they copy the diagonal for free. Every other cell is 1 + min(up-left, up, left).
Row 4 ('t'): highlighted cells are where 't' matches a letter of "sitting", so they copy the diagonal for free. Every other cell is 1 + min(up-left, up, left).
Row 5 ('e'): no letter of "sitting" matches 'e', so every cell is 1 + min(replace, delete, insert).
Row 6 ('n'): highlighted cells are where 'n' matches a letter of "sitting", so they copy the diagonal for free. Every other cell is 1 + min(up-left, up, left).
The bottom-right cell is the answer: "kitten" → "sitting" takes 3 edits.

recognitionSignals: Two strings or sequences are compared and the answer is a minimum number of operations, or a longest common something.
A choice at the END of both sequences (match them, or drop one character from either) reduces the problem to smaller prefixes of the same two sequences.
gotchas: The table is (len(a)+1) × (len(b)+1): row and column 0 represent the EMPTY prefix, which is why dp[i][j] compares a[i-1] with b[j-1].
Initialize the first row and column to 0, 1, 2, ... -- leaving them at 0 makes turning "abc" into "" look free.
On a match, don't add 1, and don't take the min with the other two either -- dp[i-1][j-1] is already optimal there.
confusableWith: Dynamic Programming: Longest Increasing Subsequence (Fundamentals) works over ONE sequence with a 1-D table; two sequences almost always mean a 2-D table like this one.
0/1 Knapsack (this track) is also a 2-D table at heart (items × capacity), but its second dimension is a budget, not a second string.

complexity.note: One O(1) cell per pair of prefixes: (n+1) × (m+1) cells. Keeping only the previous row cuts space to O(m).
